claims.text: The particles are initially solid, equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles with a nominally random solid solution.
Local chemical segregation and associated strain fields govern the onset and breadth of premelting and melting.
Increasing temperature causes minor fluctuations in elemental distribution that produce regions with different cohesive energies.
Regions with different cohesive energies act as nucleation sites for surface premelting.
Uneven local bonding strengths and strain fields lower the local energy barrier for atomic mobility.
Lower local barriers to atomic mobility broaden the premelting regime relative to a uniformly mixed particle.
Competition between surface-energy minimization and entropy stabilization drives the proposed behavior.
Particles with greater local chemical inhomogeneity will begin premelting at a lower temperature than more homogeneous particles.
Particles with greater local chemical inhomogeneity will exhibit a broader and more gradual melting transition than more homogeneous particles.
Post-synthesis annealing can be used to reduce local segregation and produce a near-ideal random solid-solution baseline.
The comparison should use otherwise comparable particle sets that differ in their degree of chemical homogeneity and are subjected to identical heating conditions.
The proposed mechanism is intended to apply primarily to sub-100 nm high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles heated in inert atmospheres without kinetic masking of intrinsic behavior.
External stress or significant oxidation may make the proposed mechanism inapplicable.
Particle-size distribution and heating rate may influence the premelting response.
Premelting onset, transition breadth, surface structural changes, and chemical maps can be measured using DSC, in-situ TEM, and EDS.
Similar premelting onset temperatures and melting profiles in the homogeneous and fluctuation-rich particle sets would falsify segregation as the governing mechanism.
